work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In illud: In qua potestate haec facis

paragraphs.text: The fear of God is the beginning of human salvation, and the law of God is the root of all the good that is in us. There is no law of God without fear, and no fear without law. The law has fear as the servant of its commands, and fear has the law as the judge of what has been commanded. So whoever approaches with fear the law and God who gave the law becomes a fellow citizen of the saints and is enrolled among the holy. But whoever scorns the fear of God and approaches the divine law with arrogance is not only found unworthy of grace but is even cast out from godliness. That is why those who approach the divine law with fear and longing are taught and enlightened in all uprightness, and learn godliness from the truth itself. They fall down before the very fountain of truth and say: "Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your statutes." This is how reverent the saints are, how much they love God, and how they learn the truth from the truth itself. But the enemies of the truth, or rather the foes of their own life, who prefer arrogance and conceit to simplicity, approach the teacher of godliness like tyrants. This is just what the children of the Jews did, as you have just heard from the words of the Gospel. When our Lord Jesus, the King of the saints, was spending time in the temple, they came up to him in the temple itself. They did not come with fitting fear, not as servants to a master, not as men to God, not even as disciples to a teacher. Enemies of the truth and hunters after wickedness, they displayed their own malice and tried to confine within human reasonings the wisdom that is above the world. For it says: "The priests and the elders of the people came to Jesus in the temple and said: By what authority are you doing these things? And who gave you this authority?" O fearless heart! How much it dares, how much it utters, how high it lifts itself in arrogance! O the folly of the wicked! O the forbearance of the Savior! The clay says these things, and the potter bears with it. The thing formed rises up against its maker, and the Benefactor, who answers to no one, patiently endures it. They demand an account from God the Word, and they pry into his authority, the very summit of sovereignty. Let us also fittingly say the words of the wise man: "O man, why are earth and ashes proud?" You question God and demand from him an account of his own works, and you dare to say to the authority that is above the world: "By what authority are you doing these things?" Why question him at all, instead of examining the power of the deeds themselves? Examine this carefully yourself in the secret council chamber of your soul. Consider the nature of the deeds, and ask whether what is happening comes from human thought, or whether what the Lord accomplishes comes from divine sovereignty. Ask the laws of nature, the limits of authority and the sequence of reasoning: what authority can raise the dead, man's or God's? Who can cleanse lepers, drive away diseases and banish every sickness of soul and body by a word alone? And again, who can fashion eyes out of clay, God or man? Why do you not ask the nature of the deeds themselves, instead of brazenly prying into the one who does them and saying: "By what authority are you doing these things?" I repeat once more the words of those who readily dare anything, who demand an account from God the Word, and who try to confine within their reasonings the one who "catches the wise in their craftiness." What folly! They put God the Word to the test of words, though every art of words and every studied web of reasoning is easily caught by him. What strength has a human word against God the Word? What can clever wickedness do against the wisdom that is above the world?

"By what authority are you doing these things?" Ask the paralytic by what authority he is raised up to health. Ask the miracles, and do not pry into the authority of the miracle-worker. Divine grace gives you no answer, because it judges those who ask with ill intent unworthy of an answer. That is how the Word of God is. When he sees a crooked and perverse soul, he shakes it off as unworthy of grace, and though it often strives hard to learn, it does not obtain truth from the Truth. The Jews ask again and again and do not learn even once. The Savior's silence tormented their souls with such anguish that the wicked council said to him then: "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." But even after these words he does not answer them, for those who asked with ill intent were unworthy of an answer. What then does the Savior say to them? "I told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? The works that I do bear witness about me." Do you see that he wants the works to be questioned, and his authority not to be pried into? The Jews ask: "If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. How long will you keep us in suspense?" And he does not resolve their doubt, for they were asking not to learn but to accuse. And the high priest Caiaphas, a fitting leader of that synagogue, reached such a pitch of madness that he said: "I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Son of the Blessed One." But the Savior, teaching us to receive words with reverence, responded to the oath but gave no resolution to the question in doubt. "Tell us," he says, "whether you are the Son of the Blessed One." The Lord says to him: "You have said so." By this acknowledgment he honored the oath, but he did not satisfy their malice, for he loathed their craftiness. The Jews sought with ill intent and received no answer. And quite rightly, for "crooked thoughts separate from God." He did not entrust his wisdom to those who pried into his wisdom with ill intent, for "wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil."

So they sought many times and did not find what they sought. But a certain woman came to him without guile and with genuine faith. She did not put his incomprehensible power to the test, but came to the Lord in simplicity, and in plain words but with genuine faith she said to him: "We know that when the Messiah, who is called Christ, comes, he will tell us everything." At once she heard from the one who loves simplicity: "I am he, the one speaking to you." She had not yet asked, and at once she learned. She had not yet sown the word of faith, and at once she reaped the fruit of godliness. For God is holy and rests upon the simple and the holy. When he sees simplicity in the one who comes to him, he too opens out freely the benefit of his wisdom; when he sees a soul twisted by wickedness, he withholds the benefit and does not grant his teaching. Listen to him saying through Moses: "If you walk uprightly toward me, I too will walk uprightly toward you. But if you walk crookedly, I too will deal with you in crooked wrath." This does not mean that the divine nature bends its own uprightness, but that the things of the truth do not come straight to the wicked. "By what authority are you doing these things? Or who gave you this authority?" And the Savior [?] them. Pay attention here to how the Lord of all lays down for us a rule and a standard of teaching. What is it? He wants us not to answer every question put to us by wicked heretics, whether Jews or Greeks or any others who have cut themselves off from godliness. For it often happens, it really does, that people ask questions that do not deserve an answer. To such worthless questions one must by all means respond with a just counter-question. That is why the Lord says to them: "I too will ask you one question. If you tell me, I too will answer you. The baptism of John, where did it come from? From heaven or from men?" See, I ask you, how the fountain of wisdom exposes falsehood by a question. See how the Word of God overturns wickedness by reasoning. And observe too how wickedness is destroyed by its own arrows and dragged down by its own evil devices. "The baptism of John, where did it come from? From heaven or from men?" They weighed the force of the question among themselves and said: "If we say, From heaven, he will say to us, Why then did you not believe him?" Wickedness knows where it will slip. It knows that it is undone by the very things it puts forward. Since they had not obeyed John, they were afraid to say that it was from God, lest refutation follow on their heels. "But if we say, From men, we fear the crowd, that we may be stoned." For the people's high regard for the righteous man will bring a punishment on us that cannot be escaped. "For all the people held John to be a prophet." So they did not want to tell the truth, that it was from God, for they had shaken off the truth of God; yet they did not dare to tell a lie either. Their shamelessness was held in check by fear, and that not divine fear but human. And that is how it is: many who do not have the fear of God are often slaves to human fear. They feared the people. If only they had feared God and not the people! The one would have been godliness; the other is ungodliness. "They say to him: We do not know." See how wickedness lurks in the wicked. See how ungodliness proclaims its own perversity. Like a viper or one of the most vicious beasts lurking in holes under the ground, which pokes its head quietly out of its burrow but will not come out altogether, so the Jews, who live in the den of wickedness, do not bring their own opinion out into the light. That is why the Lord says to them: "Neither will I tell you." See how his silence punished the perverse question. See how he did not satisfy their wickedness, but left them stranded in the middle of their reasonings. What once happened to Balaam's donkey because of the angel who stood in its way, that is what happened to the wickedness of the Jews. It dared not turn to the right, toward the truth, because of the Savior's refusal, nor to the left, toward falsehood, because of their fear of the people.

So we too, brothers, must take this rule from the Lord and not yield on everything to the questions of heretics. When a heretic asks a question with ill intent, answer his perverse inquiry with a just counter-question. A heretic will often ask: "Do you know God or not?" If you say, "I know him," he immediately goes on: "So you know what you worship?" "Yes," says the godly man, for who could bear to say, "I worship what I do not know"? Again he goes on: "Then do you know the essence of God?" If you say, "I do not know it," he immediately objects: "Then you do not know what you worship." See, I ask you, these crooked words; see the wiles of these wicked serpents. Do you see? But there is no need to be disturbed. For you must know this, brothers: there are many ways of knowing. One can know that God is without knowing how he is. Even among us human beings there are many paths to knowledge. I know that a certain man lives in a certain city, but I do not know what trade he follows. I know that another man follows a certain trade, but I do not know where his family comes from. I know in part and in part I am ignorant. And certainly partial knowledge does not amount to complete knowledge, nor does not knowing everything cancel out partial knowledge. What then? I know that God is, that he is good, that he is immortal, that he is incorruptible, that he is beyond conception, that he is incomprehensible, that he is incorporeal, that he is unchangeable. All this I know, and knowing it I worship. But how he is I do not know, nor was I taught to pry into how he is, but only that he is. I find no greater teacher than the apostle, none who can set godliness before me better. With a ringing voice he teaches us something like this: "Whoever comes to God must believe that he is"—not how he is, but that he is—"and that he rewards those who seek him." So I worship what I know. I did not learn to pry into the essence of God. I learned to believe, brothers: to believe, not to pry. Read over your own confession, heretic, the one you agreed to in the hidden and awesome mystery. When you came to be baptized, what did you say? Were you inquiring, prying, investigating, or were you believing? You came in a different spirit, and you were deemed worthy of that grace on other terms. If indeed you were deemed worthy while thinking such things, then you have broken the covenant: at the awesome and dread mysteries you brought faith, but once outside the mysteries you set limits to faith and bring in inquiry instead.

But see what the enemy of the truth says: "Has God given us reasoning for no purpose? Did we receive the mind's power of judgment for nothing? Faith too must be examined by reasoning, and piety must not go unexamined." Very well. But the limit of the examination is the divine oracles and the rules of piety that he has given us. You, however, overstep the rules. You do not keep in line with the divinely inspired Scriptures; you pry into divine things, you do violence to the truth, and everywhere you are eager to follow the unevenness of your reasonings rather than to serve faith, as though you had mastered the experience of everything else, or had come to know all the other things that are seen. Tell me, using your chain of reasoning, how the heaven stands, vaulted to such boundless height and having nothing anywhere in so vast a circuit to support it. How does it stand? What holds it up? What are the foundations on which it is fixed? How is it that in so long a time its beauty does not dissolve and its harmony is not destroyed? Show me the columns that bear it; show me the base that lies beneath such masses. But why speak of heaven and not of the earth I tread on? First explain to me how the earth is set. That it is founded upon the waters I too have been taught, and you yourself confess it. But explain how it is fixed upon the waters. Do not simply follow the statement; give a reasoned account of what is asked. How are so many and such great mountains, hills and plains borne upon the waters? Tell me how the sea is bounded; tell me how the sea that rages with so many waves and crests to boundless height breaks up once it comes near the sand. Explain, brother, how, though the earth is one, one mother, the things that grow from it are diverse: where the bitter roots come from, where the sweet, where the differences among fruits. One earth that brings forth, one rain that nourishes: where does the difference come from? Explain where the springs gushed forth from, and out of what depths, and how it is possible to grasp these things. But when we are at a loss over such things, we have one true and pious solution to our perplexities. Blessed David sang it, saying something like this: "For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith." The works cannot be grasped without faith, and yet God can be found without faith? The works not without faith, and the Son by demonstration? "For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith." But let us leave the enemies of the truth and return to the sound and secure ground of faith, and show the rule of piety shining forth through truth itself. No one among the ancients is more trustworthy than Moses; no one among those of the new covenant is wiser than Paul. Search the old dispensation and you will find no one greater than Moses: "For I know you, and you have found favor beyond all." No one in the new is more perfect than Paul, for he is a chosen vessel and has Christ speaking within him. Do not overstep the bounds of Moses and of Paul. What did Moses find: comprehension of the essence, or the glory of God? Moses, brothers, came to desire God as a man who loved God. He did not realize that he was desiring the impossible, yet he made it plain by what he asked of God. For what does he say? "I beseech you, Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, let me see you clearly; show yourself to me." He was a brother of Philip, who said, "Show us the Father, and it is enough for us." "Lord, you said, 'You have found favor in my sight'; show yourself to me, that I may see you clearly." He had seen him in the bush; he had seen him on Mount Sinai; he had seen him appearing in various places and displaying his manifestation in various ways. But that blessed Moses longed to see him, the very stamp of his nature. Being a man, he imagined human things about the power that is above the world. God accepted the longing of his faithful servant, and he persuades the human appetite that desires the impossible. For what does he say to him? "No one shall see my face and live." The capacity of those who long cannot contain the object of their longing; mortal sight cannot bear the immortal nature. What then, O Master? Do you leave his longing unconsoled, and give not even a shadow of what he desires to one who conceives so great a longing? Hence he says: "I will set you on the rock and cover you with my hand; and as my glory passes by, you will see my back, but my front you will not see." "As it passes by": he did not say "I," but "my glory." For it is not possible to pass beyond the glory and find the essence. Moses found nothing beyond glory, and he did not see even this in full, but only its back. This is not because the divine nature is outlined with a back and a chest, for it is simple and uncompounded, but because God makes himself known in this way, not according to the dignity that befits him, but according to the capacity of those who are to enjoy the sight. Moses reached the glory and did not pass beyond the glory. And you, heretic, pass beyond the glory and pry into the essence of God? Let us come also to blessed Paul. Paul, in the new dispensation, after peering into certain particular dispensations of God, as if growing dizzy at the depths of the thought, cried out that great utterance full of amazement, saying something like this: "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that it should be repaid to him?" And the end of the passage: "For from him and through him and to him are all things; to him be glory forever." Do you see that when he came to the glory of God he did not overstep the bound? And why speak of human beings? Ascend in thought to the things above the world. Ask the heavens and say: "What can you tell me about God? Heavens, describe to me what kind of being God is; tell me what God is in essence." But the heavens do not answer when asked about impossible things. And even if you boldly ask this, that divine oracle will answer you through the wonderful Jeremiah: "Heaven shuddered at this." For heaven truly shudders when it sees the divine nature being pried into. Blessed David too will strike back, rebuking this measureless curiosity, and will say: "Have you not heard that the heavens declare, not the nature of God, but the glory of God?" Did he not cry out to you on his holy harp that "the heavens declare the glory of God," not the nature of God? They do not interpret the essence; they announce the glory. And do not think that the powers above the world know anything more. Ask the angels. Ask, I say, not because you are permitted to converse with the powers above, but because you have from Scripture the remedies and the means to muzzle your audacity. Ask the angels; ask when you see them dancing on earth or singing hymns. Say to them: "What new thing do you teach? What strange thing do you announce?" And at once the divine choir will answer you through the divine Gospels: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men." Angels came to earth and did not overstep the bounds of glory; and heretics did not hesitate to overstep them. But what of the highest powers, those above the angels, I mean? I mean those of the archangels, and those are distinct natures. Ask the cherubim, the royal throne: "You who are seated upon the cherubim, appear!" Ask the cherubim, as a throne of sapphire with one seated on the throne like the likeness of a son of man. And there came a voice of the cherubim, crying out like the sound of many waters: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place."

Do you see the reverence of the cherubim too? They reached the glory and did not overstep the bound. "Blessed be the glory of the Lord." And how? "From his place," to show you that he dwells even in the heavenly places and lies far above them, higher in dignity than the heavenly and invisible powers. They do not speak as those who draw near, but as those who stand far off from the divine dignity. "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place." Not that he has a place, for he encompasses all things in place; but it calls the dignity that surrounds him "the place of God." You have seen the voice of the cherubim too: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord." And it announced nothing more. For you must learn God's proclamations from those who stand around him, and the seraphim stood around him. What, then, can be learned from them? Do not hinder [us]. They too will say: "Though we excel in dignity, we recognize the bounds of our nature and do not leap over the measures of knowledge. We do not pry into our Creator; we do not busy ourselves with the one who honored us. We know that the incomprehensible nature is not subject to inquiry and is not enslaved to chains of reasoning. The glory of the one who is worshiped transcends at once every angelic state, every thought above the world, and every power above the heavens. That is why we too do not overstep the bounds." The cherubim did not overstep them, but with all reverence they sing that heavenly hymn: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory." Do Paul and Moses not put you to shame, since they did not overstep the glory? Heaven will put you to shame, announcing the glory. But heaven does not persuade you? The angels will put you to shame. But you despise angels? Fear the cherubim. But you overstep these too in your daring? Let the seraphim bring you to your senses. But you are persuaded neither by examples above the world nor by earthly ones? Then go outside the sacred choirs; banish yourself from the divine courts. For you cannot pry into God and be numbered among the faithful. And why speak of God? Do you not know that it is a fearful thing to make bold to search out the nature of God? If you want to pry even into the works of God themselves, God does not count you worthy of his intimacy, but casts you far off as one who makes bold at the impossible. Moses, a man of such greatness and stature, the worker of so many wonders, who became mediator between God and men, for whom the sea was divided, who brought down the manna from heaven: this man, because he dared to measure a single one of God's commands by human reasoning and did not yield to the divine power, received a penalty from which there was no appeal. For when he came to the rock, he said to the people: "O hard and disobedient people, shall I be able to give you water out of this rock?" And what did God say to him? "Because you did not glorify me before the congregation, you shall not enter the land that I swore to give." Here pay close attention, I beg you. "Because you did not glorify me." What would glorifying have been? To say: "God can do all things." For it is a sin against God to examine by reasoning the things he does, and not to yield to the divine power that accomplishes its works beyond all things. David defends Moses, who slipped not in mind but in tongue. For the sins of the righteous lie on the lips, but the wrongdoings of the ungodly lie in the mind. And just as the ungodly man is cut off in mind yet seems somehow to draw near to God with his lips ("For this people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me"), so the godly man, though his heart is sound, often slips with his tongue. That is why David defends Moses, prophet speaking for prophet: "They provoked him at the water of contradiction, and Moses suffered harm because of them." Not because of himself. What does "because of them" mean? He did not show unbelief of his own accord; but, troubled by the people's contradiction, he no longer found his reasoning clear, being as it were in confusion. I have said this in answer to what is put forward by the workshop of unrighteousness. Where did you hear of "unbegotten" and "begotten"? Where did you hear those frenzied and fantastical ways of arguing? The things of the Spirit were set aside, and the things of the devil brought in in their place. If you seek these things, why do you claim Paul as your teacher? If you pry into these things, why do you pride yourself on having Peter? Deny the faith, then, and put forward inquiry instead. "But I do not depart from Scripture," he says. "God forbid!" An enemy, and a disciple, and an introducer of reasonings? Explain to me, since you are a slave to reasoning, how the Savior came in when the doors were shut. What need is there to busy ourselves with the other questions? Often they bring harm both to those who speak and to those who listen. Should I ask you to explain the invisible nature: how the Father begot, what the manner of the divine generation is? What I demand concerns the dispensation.

Tell me how the Savior came in when the doors were shut. How did the body come in? The nature of a body contradicts the Gospels; if I follow faith, the truth cannot lie. How did he come in when the doors were shut? It was not the bodiless nature alone, which passes through the bodies of all things; the body was there together with the bodiless nature, and it was the instrument of the bodiless nature. For the Savior had this human body. Indeed, the disciples, looking at the strangeness of the miracle, thought that he was a spirit, since what was before them surpassed the nature of a body. [?] he says to them as they doubted: "Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have." How did he come in? Did the planks dissolve like air? Or was the body made thin and so passed through the thickness of the wood? But neither can you say, nor am I able to explain. Scripture has handed down none of these things to me. I do not pry; I follow what it has proclaimed, even against my own inclination. I believe that he came in; how he did so I do not pry into. Do not suppose that he came in through [opened] doors [?]. It did not say that he came in when the door had grown porous or had dissolved, but "when the doors were shut." It proclaimed what happened; it did not show the manner of what happened. Peter came out of prison. But the gates were opened for him, and Scripture noted this, saying that the iron gate opened for them of its own accord. It did not say: "Of its own accord it let Peter pass through." For his body was human and made of human dough. Christ's body, however, was human because of its kinship with us, but divine both because of its union with God the Word and because of the Virgin's wondrous childbearing. How did he come in when the doors were shut? How did he go up when the heavens were shut? Oh, the absurdity of those who dare such things! Oh, the piety of those who believe all! But what does the opponent say? "We do not find faith secure everywhere; we have found it slipping too. One must not believe without examination, but with careful examination." And many of those outside agree with them. For the views of the heretics and of the pagans are kindred: the latter are the inventions of demons, and the former the teachings of demons. So some of those who oppose the faith say that its lack of reasoning is harmful, and that unless examined reasoning is joined to faith, it brings the believer no profit anywhere. "Where," he says, "do you want to examine the nature of faith from? Do you want to start from the very beginning, from creation itself? Look at the one you call the first-formed man: I find him fallen through faith." See the words of the evil demon, who lightly dares to attempt anything: what he dares, what he utters, what he puts forward! "You say," he says, "that the serpent said to him, 'On whatever day you eat of the tree, you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.' He believed the serpent, and by believing he perished. So faith is the beginning of evils." This is what those enemies of the truth, those foes of piety, say to us. But the impious have not understood the true definition of faith; they do not know what they are putting forward. Do we say that everyone who believes anything at all has faith and is proclaimed faithful? It is not the one who believes just anyone who is faithful, but the one who truly believes God. Did you show that he perished by believing God? He fell by believing the devil; he slipped by disbelieving God. Why do you twist the words? Hear Jeremiah saying: "Hear me, you who hate judgment and pervert all that is right." Surely you should have said: "Unbelief is the beginning of evils." For if he had believed God when he said, "On whatever day you eat, you shall surely die," he would not have slipped, but would have had faith, a faith secure unto salvation. Never slander the name of faith. It is not the one who believes everything who is faithful, but the one who believes God: he alone both is and is called faithful. Leave off inquiries and embrace faith. Faith illumines all things; faith sanctifies all things; faith makes one worthy of the Holy Spirit. For Stephen was full of faith and power. Had faith not shone out first, power would not have followed the saint. Where there is faith, there is power too; where there is unbelief, there is weakness too. Faith is the beginning of good things; faith is the fount of good things. Let us take up the weapon of salvation. Why do you enslave yourself to words and flee the truth? Why do you put forward things that not even the nature of angels dares to search out? Why do I say the nature of angels? Things that not even demons dare. You will not follow Peter? You will not follow Paul? Not the angels? Not the cherubim? Then at least become a disciple of the demons. The demons saw the Savior and said to him: "Ah, what have we to do with you, Son of God?" The demons confess the Son, and you, heretic, blaspheme? Demons make him equal, and you contrive inequality? "And what am I to do," says the heretic, "when the Lord says, 'That they may know you, the only true God'? He said 'only'; he proclaimed the Father the only true God. I keep in line with the truth announced by God." You follow the word "only" and are enslaved to the expression? Then keep to the rules for me in the matters under examination. God says through the prophet: "I am the first, and I am hereafter, and there is no other besides me. There is no righteous one and savior besides me. Turn to me, and you shall be saved, from the ends of the earth. I am God, and there is no other. By myself I swear." "I am the first, and I am hereafter." And he added: "And there is no other besides me." Do you see how he points to a solitary nature that has nothing in common with any other, separate nature? It is God who says this: "I am, and there is no other"; he who says through the prophet: "I stretched out the heaven alone." Pay attention to "alone," since you cite "the only true God." "I stretched out the heaven alone." And here likewise: "I am, and there is no other. By myself I swear." Pay attention both to the authority and to the power of the speaker: he said, "There is no other," and "I alone am," and "this I swore by myself." And this indicates that there is no one greater than he who speaks. So the apostle too says: "Since he had no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself." So he has no one greater who says: "By myself I swear: righteousness shall go forth from my mouth; my words shall not be turned back." And what do you swear? "That to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess the true God." Who is saying this, heretic? The Father or the Son? For me, a believer, and for every pious person, the Father's dignity is also the Son's authority. Keep this in mind: much of what we say is proclaimed polemically, not dogmatically. For me and for every believer the doctrine of piety stands firm, that where the Father alone speaks, the Son and the Holy Spirit are included as well. Where the Son speaks, there is the Father's authority; where the Father exercises authority, there is the Son's power; where the Holy Spirit works, there is the Father's working. The glory of the Holy Trinity is not divided, because the doctrine of the truth is not divided. Do you not confess one kingdom?

Since I am training myself against the enemy, I have said these things, so that none of those who love to slander may say, "See how he said that everything belongs to the Son, and that it is the Son who speaks, and so he made the prophecy foreign to the Father and proper to the Son." For me the rule of faith stands unshaken. What is being practised here is a contest. Here I show the Son speaking, and once I have convinced you, I hold to my own conviction: the Father speaks, the Son proclaims, the Holy Spirit utters the oracle. "I am first, and I am also hereafter, and besides me there is no God. I swear by myself." Who is it who says, "I am, and there is no other," and, "Righteousness shall go forth from my mouth, and my words shall not be turned back; for to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess the true God"? How do you take the saying? To whom do you apply the name? But you should not declare what you do not know, and I do not promise what I do not understand. Let us follow a spiritual teacher who can guide us toward godliness. So do not listen to me; listen with me. I know Paul as the teacher of the Church's doctrines. When I say Paul, I proclaim Christ, for it was he who spoke in Paul, as it is said: "Since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me." Paul applies to Christ this prophecy of Isaiah quoted earlier: "I am, and there is no other," and, "I swear by myself that to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess the true God." And where do you find this proof? Writing to the Romans he says: "Why do you judge your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? Why do you judge one another? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess the true God." He is the one who says, "I am, and there is no other; I swear by myself that to me every knee shall bow." Paul refers the prophecy to Christ. The one speaking in the prophet is Christ, and Christ says, "I alone am, and there is no other." Does he then exclude the Father from the Godhead? No, he does not exclude him, just as indeed he does not, for the glory is undivided. It has therefore been clearly shown that when the Son says, "I alone am," he does not exclude the Father. In the same way, when he says of the Father, "that they may know you, the only true God," he does not cut himself off from the truth. And this passage does more than heal the difficulty. From this very testimony comes the proof that Christ is true God, for it goes on: "And every tongue shall confess the true God." So the one who says "I alone" and "I am true" is the Son. What difference do the words make, then, when the truth is in agreement? Why, then, did he say, "you, the only true God"? Be taught, and do not fight. The Saviour is the teacher of the world and the corrector of the whole earth. He raises what has fallen, turns back what has gone astray, and renews what has grown old. He knew that his word would go forth and prevail throughout all that is under heaven, to correct the error of the Greeks and to refute the disobedience of the Jews. So he puts forward a two-edged word. By calling God "the true and only" one, he exposes the many gods who falsely bear the name. By adding "and Jesus Christ whom you have sent," he refutes those who deny the dispensation. And so that you may learn, brother, that he is both true God and Son of the true God, consider John the evangelist. These words are written by him, for the Gospel according to John contains "that they may know you, the only true God." That very herald who proclaimed these things also writes in his own epistle. The first epistle is one of those read in the church, not one of the apocrypha. The fathers exclude the second and third from the canon, but all have agreed that the first epistle is John's. We must therefore pay attention to what that saint proclaims about God in the epistle. "We know," he says, "that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true one; and we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life." This same man, brothers, both said those words and proclaimed these. Now, if you please, let us reflect further on the word "alone" and contend over it. Let many arrows be shot at the unbeliever, not to wound bodies but to correct minds. Let words be sent to the faithful, but arrows to the faithless. "Your arrows are sharp, O mighty one; peoples will fall beneath you; they pierce the heart of the enemies." So says blessed Jeremiah, or rather his disciple Baruch, as Elisha was Elijah's disciple: "He who prepared the earth for all time filled it with cattle and four-footed beasts. He sends out the light, and it goes; he called it, and it obeyed him with trembling. The stars shone in their watches and rejoiced." "He called them," that is, the stars, he says, "and they said, 'Here we are'; and they shone with gladness for him who made them." And after saying so much about God, he says: "This is our God; no other shall be compared with him." Notice carefully how he shuts out any other: "No other shall be compared with him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterwards he appeared on earth and lived among men." This is our God, with whom no other shall be compared, who afterwards appeared on earth and lived among men. Do you see how secure the truth is? See how it leaves no opening for error. A Jew cannot slander the truth by saying that it was to Moses that God appeared, since God appeared on the mountain. Besides him there is no other, yet he does not exclude the Father from the divine dignity. If the Father is called "alone," does he banish the Son from sharing that dignity? When God says that he alone is the one, whether he is the Father or the Son, he does not deny that he shares his own nature with the other. The Father does not exclude the Son; the Son does not set aside the Father. When such things are said, the words are aimed at the error of idolatry. Why do you contrive blasphemy against the Only-begotten? God does not give his glory to idols. Does he then refuse it to the one begotten of him as well? No, he gives it to him, and not merely by grace but because they share one nature. And where is the proof that Christ receives the Father's glory? For he said, "My glory I will not give to another."

Hear how the Saviour himself, speaking with the apostles, says, "When the Son of Man comes in the glory of his Father." Yet the Father had said beforehand, "My glory I will not give to another." Search the words and you will find the meaning. He did not say, "My glory I will not give to my Son," but "I will not give it to another." "Another" means one who is foreign to that kinship and cut off from that nature. But the Son is not another, "for I and the Father are one." It has therefore been clearly shown that "that they may know you, the only true God" does not do away with the Son's being true God. Do not slander the argument as though its meaning had been left hanging. That is what happened to some of the brothers concerning the cup. They brought their charges as if the meaning had received no solution. "He left the inquiry," they say, "suspended and hanging." But what more was there to say, brothers? What further proof was needed beyond what had already been said? First there was the saying, "If it is possible, let the cup pass from me," and what its wording suggests, for the wording seems in some way to place the one praying under another's authority. Beside it we set that other saying of the Lord, which is truly full of all divine authority and displays the dignity of the speaker: "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up." We showed that "I have" belongs properly to the Godhead, while "If it is possible, let this cup pass from me" was spoken in the person of the flesh and not in the person of the Godhead. On these points we again set the Master's own testimony as a seal, for that is why he said, "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." And we pointed out that it is utterly absurd for us to throw the lowliness of the saying onto the authority of the Godhead when the Lord himself ascribes it to the flesh. We also set out the Lord's purpose, the reason he said, "Let the cup pass from me." He was not declining death in order to escape the dispensation of the cross. He used this expression because those ignorant of the dispensation were going to stumble at the cross. And again the testimony that followed bore out this sense: "Pray that you may not enter into temptation." Others have slandered us, claiming that we said, "If it is possible to fulfil the dispensation by another manner of death." This was never said and never will be. I did not say "by another death." I said "that the dispensation might be fulfilled in another way," that is, without death. For I was explaining the cup, and I took "otherwise" to mean "without death." And this took place not because the Lord was truly declining to die for the world. He was confirming the weakness of the flesh, showing that it was truly flesh that feared and was troubled. "For the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." He ascribed the words of weakness to the flesh; he did not wound the authority of the Godhead. Why do you slander what I do not say? Why do you misrepresent what I do not preach? I spoke of another way, not of death but of the dispensation. For it was not said, "If it is possible, let this cup be exchanged." The weakness belongs to the flesh; the suffering belongs to the incarnation. He speaks the words of weakness to show that he has put on this nature which fears death. And so that you would not again be enslaved to the wording, I went further and added this as well: what reason could there be for the apostles to trample death nobly while the Lord of the apostles feared and trembled at the experience of death? I will say this now too, brothers. Paul boldly declares that he is ready not only to be bound but even to die for the name of Christ. Would Paul's Lord then decline death? Is Paul's heart not shattered while Christ's soul is troubled? For he says, "Now my soul is troubled." I said all this to you before witnesses. Does it not persuade you? Does "if it is possible" still make you stumble? "Yes," he says. Let us meet the contentious man, brothers. Let us strive by the power of truth to raise up those who have fallen through the weakness of unbelief. He objects: "If Christ had authority, he would not have said, 'If it is possible, let it pass.'" Then you must accuse God as well, for in the law he used an expression far removed from his own authority. He spoke to Moses from Mount Sinai in that great and fearful manifestation, when all the people trembled as they heard the voice of the living God. Then God, who holds authority over all, governs all things for all, and gives all things, says to Moses: "Who will grant that their heart may be such that they fear me and keep [?] all their days, so that it may go well with them and with their children?" God says, "Who will give this people a heart?" And who, O Master, is mightier than you, that he could give it? Are you not the one who gives all things, and above all the things that lead to godliness? If you were not the one who gives a good heart to those who love you, if you are not the giver, how can David pray to you, "Create a clean heart in me, O God"? The prophets ask you for a clean heart, for the other good gifts, and for purity of heart. Yet you use a human expression and say, "Who will give this people a heart?" And who gives more than you do? But even if you, being good, spoke this way, blessed Moses did not follow your wording. He proclaimed your dignity, showed your authority, and made your sovereignty known. In Deuteronomy he says to the people: "The Lord your God has given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this very day."

Do you see that one and the same God gives the heart, the eyes, the ears and everything else? How, then, could the one who gives everything say, "Who will give this people such a heart?" And again, if he were not the one who gives a heart, how could he say through Ezekiel, "I will tear the heart of stone out of them and give them a heart of flesh, and I will write my law on their hearts"? There God himself, who is able to give a good heart, says, "Who will give?" In the same way the Only-begotten of the Father fills the world with his authority and says with authority, "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up." Yet in his human form he answers again, speaking in the person of the flesh in its weakness: "If it is possible, let the cup pass from me." So do not misrepresent what was not said, but keep in step with what is preached. Do not slander the teaching when you have not grasped its meaning. I know how you slip into slander; I know where this affliction of yours comes from. The passion is human; the disease is envy. When the eye is clean, it sees and discerns everything rightly. But if smoke gets into it and spoils the beauty of its sight, or dust falls into it, its sight is dulled, and it no longer sees well, as it saw rightly before. So it is now with each of the hearers. As long as he has a clean eye of faith and a clean eyelid of love, he sees rightly and clearly. But if the smoke of blasphemy gets into what is said, or the dust of envy creeps into the soul, it clouds his sight and destroys the purity of his mind. Then he hears what he did not hear, and what he did hear he understands badly. The divine Scripture foresaw the stumbling of those whose minds would stumble over the sacred writings. That is why one of the prophets, after completing his divine message, cried out: "Who is wise, and will understand these things? Who is prudent, and will know them? For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them." So do not twist words into stumbling blocks, brother. The word is plain; the truth is plain. It was not one listener who heard it, not a second, not a tenth, not a hundredth, but a boundless, countless multitude. The Church is a sea of godliness, filled not with waves but with faith. Among us the ship of teaching is not wrecked, not battered, not tossed about, not caught in storms. It comes to anchor, as in a calm harbour, in the souls of those who love the Lord. But enough of this. What we must consider is that the saints of God are exposed to slander. What wonder is it, then, if we are slandered, we who are cheap and lowly and nothing, so to speak? Have you not heard how David says, "Deliver me from the slander of men"? The holy apostles of the Saviour were also slandered, as blessed Paul said: "And why not do as we are slandered, and as some claim we say, 'Let us do evil so that good may come'?" I am not grieved to be slandered along with the saints, even though I am unworthy of the saints. I have all of you as my judges, and before all of you our common father, who does not judge by prejudice but gives his verdict with understanding. He knows our thoughts, and he recognises our words too, for it was from him that we learned these things. We put it to you: if anything in what was said had been lacking, he would have corrected it; but he raised no objection [?]. And if he had corrected it, he would have done so not out of hatred but out of love. For a father reproves the one he loves, and turns away from the one he does not correct. But this admirable father both welcomes what is well said and applies correction to what is mistaken. This is a father's proper task: to give the prize to what is well said and preached with faith. His verdict, then, suffices in place of all others, and above his stands the verdict of the all-holy God. Let us hold fast to godliness and keep the faith unshaken. Believe the truth and do not contradict the truth. Do not set limits to the faith. Do not pry into the divine nature. Do not subject the immortal dignity to mortal reasonings. The road of reasoning is treacherous; the understanding that comes from confessing the faith is secure and firm. Faith is true wisdom. Hear what the divine oracle says: "Even if someone is perfect among the sons of men, without the wisdom that comes from you he will be counted as nothing." Flee disputes, and do not prefer words to faith. Have Paul as your teacher; enrol under Peter as your guide; follow their faith. Hear Peter saying, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Follow Paul, who clearly sings the praises of the Son of God. In one place he says that "God has spoken to us in a Son, through whom he also made the ages. He is the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his being, and he upholds all things by the word of his power." In another place, speaking of the Jews, he proclaims: "To them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, comes the Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever and ever. Amen."
